title: How To Handle Students Who Beg You Not To Hold Them Accountable
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the difficult moment when a genuinely remorseful student pleads to be let off the hook, arguing that giving in — however sympathetic the impulse — opens the door to more pleading in the future and breeds resentment among students held to consistent standards. He advises committing fully to following the classroom management plan without hesitation, since any visible wavering invites more intense pleading, and recommends walking away immediately after delivering a consequence to avoid prolonged negotiation. For situations where a student follows up afterward, he offers scripted honest responses that acknowledge sympathy while explaining the fairness rationale for not making exceptions. Linsin closes with an anecdote about students who later thank him for being fair despite their in-the-moment frustration, framing consistent accountability, not leniency, as the truer form of care.
points: Giving in to a remorseful student's pleading, however sympathetic, invites more pleading in the future and breeds resentment among consistently-held students.
Visible hesitation when considering an exception makes students push harder; committing fully and immediately to the consequence is the more effective response.
Walking away promptly after delivering a consequence prevents prolonged negotiation or argument.
When a student follows up afterward, honest scripted responses ('I'd have to do the same for everybody else') acknowledge sympathy while explaining the fairness rationale.
Students frequently return later in the year to thank teachers for being fair with them, even after initially resisting accountability in the moment.
quotes: They plead. They beg. They petition. They dramatize, beseech, and implore with puppy-dog eyes.
Well, for starters, you’ll open the floodgates to more and more pleading and pressuring every time you try to enforce a consequence.
Because as soon as that student sees you thinking about it, they’re going to lay it on even thicker and heavier. And every second that passes will make it that much harder to follow through.
I wish I could, but if I let you get away with it, then I’d have to do the same for everybody else.
What still surprises me is how many students approach me later in the year to shake my hand and thank me for being fair with them.
It also makes it that much easier to say no, to follow through, to do the right thing. To be the leader they need, not the weak-kneed friend they don’t.
